strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and practically useful idea: restricting OSM watermarking to a specific sub-domain to simultaneously preserve generation quality/persistence (unlike full-coverage watermarks) while retaining the strong statistical guarantees of watermark-based detection for fingerprinting purposes.

Clearly articulates a set of practical desiderata for fingerprinting (reliability, persistence, stealthiness, harmlessness, robustness) grounded in prior work, and systematically evaluates the method against each.

Extensive empirical evaluation across two model families (Llama3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-3B/7B) and three domains (Math, Health, French), covering detection reliability with formal p-value guarantees, quality preservation (perplexity, GPT-4 judge, benchmark accuracy), persistence under multiple finetuning scenarios, and robustness to system prompts/sampling strategies.

Direct empirical comparison against two backdoor-based fingerprinting baselines (instructional fingerprinting, scalable fingerprinting), showing clear practical advantages in robustness to system prompts and persistence under finetuning — this strengthens the paper's claims of superiority over existing approaches.

Rich set of supplementary analyses in the appendix (watermark tokens as domain triggers, multiple simultaneous watermark keys, domain-leakage sensitivity study, watermarking a harmful-content domain) that explore the boundaries and practical considerations of the approach, going beyond a minimal viable evaluation.

Good use of the monotonicity property of watermark-based statistics to argue that detection power can be recovered via additional queries even when signal is weakened, which is empirically demonstrated.
weaknesses: The method's core threat model implicitly assumes the adversary will naturally be queried/triggered into generating target-domain content; if a deployer restricts or filters domain-specific queries (intentionally or not) or the domain never naturally arises in their use case, the fingerprint may never be triggered — this fundamental limitation is not deeply analyzed.

Persistence against in-domain (worst-case adversarial) finetuning degrades substantially, and for the Math domain on Qwen2.5-3B the paper explicitly states the signal cannot be recovered at all even with more queries — a nontrivial gap not fully resolved by the monotonicity argument.

Sensitivity to domain leakage between regularization and target datasets is a real limitation acknowledged by the authors; in practice, guaranteeing clean separation for arbitrary real-world domains may be difficult, and this could undermine the harmlessness/specificity guarantees.

Only one watermarking scheme (KGW logit-distillation) is evaluated; generalization to other OSM watermarking families (weight-perturbation, joint classifier-based) mentioned in related work is not empirically tested.

Model scale is modest (1B–7B parameters); it is unclear whether findings (e.g., ease of domain-specific behavior learning, quality preservation) transfer to larger, more capable open models that are more likely to be commercially valuable targets for fingerprinting.

Stealthiness claims rely on qualitative examples and comparison rather than a rigorous quantitative detectability/distinguishability metric against an adaptive adversary attempting to identify or filter domain-specific watermark queries.

No evaluation against more sophisticated/adaptive adversaries (e.g., model deployers aware of the domain-specific watermarking technique who might specifically try to suppress or filter suspected trigger domains), which is a realistic concern given the threat model of restrictive licensing disputes.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically important and timely problem (model provenance for open-source/openly-weighted LLMs) and provides a clear, well-motivated taxonomy of desiderata for fingerprinting methods (reliability, persistence, stealthiness, harmlessness, robustness) that is useful as a frame of reference for the field.

The core idea—restricting watermark distillation to a provider-chosen sub-domain rather than the full output distribution—is a sensible and reasonably novel repurposing of existing OSM watermarking techniques (KGW distillation) to address a different problem (fingerprinting vs. content provenance), and is simple to understand and implement.

The empirical evaluation is broad in scope: it covers reliability/p-values vs. number of queries, generation quality (perplexity and GPT-4-judge) both in- and out-of-domain, standard benchmark accuracy, persistence under four different finetuning distributions (including an adversarial worst-case where finetuning occurs on the watermark domain itself), robustness to several system prompts and sampling strategies, and qualitative stealthiness examples.

The paper includes direct, carefully constructed comparisons against two prior backdoor-based fingerprinting baselines (instructional fingerprinting, scalable fingerprinting), showing that these baselines are much more brittle to system prompts and finetuning — this comparative evidence is a plausible selling point of the proposed approach.

A reasonably rich set of ablations is provided in the appendix (KGW hyperparameters, watermark tokens as domain triggers, multiple co-existing watermark keys, domain leakage in regularization data, and watermarking of a 'harmful content' domain), which helps probe the boundaries and failure modes of the method rather than only showing favorable results.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is fairly incremental: the method is essentially the existing KGW logit-distillation watermark (Gu et al.) applied with a domain-restricted training/regularization split and a new regularization loss term; the conceptual leap from 'OSM watermark' to 'domain-specific OSM watermark for fingerprinting' is useful but not a particularly deep methodological innovation.

There is an unresolved internal inconsistency: the main text and setup (Sec. 5) state the second base model is QWEN2.5-7B-INSTRUCT, while essentially all tables and figures (Table 1, Table 2, Fig. 2–4, App. A) refer to QWEN2.5-3B. This raises concerns about experimental rigor/proofreading and leaves it unclear which model was actually used.

The threat model explicitly lists quantization as a plausible model modification an adversary might perform, yet the persistence/robustness evaluation only tests finetuning and system prompts — quantization (and other common real-world transformations such as model merging, pruning, or distillation into a different architecture) are never empirically evaluated, leaving a stated threat largely untested.

The domain-leakage ablation (App. C.3) shows that even modest overlap (10%+) between the regularization dataset and the target domain significantly degrades domain specificity (increasing false positive rate), which is a serious practical concern given that real-world regularization/finetuning corpora are rarely cleanly disjoint from any given target domain (e.g., health or French content can appear incidentally in general web corpora); this undermines the claimed reliability/harmlessness guarantees in realistic settings more than the paper acknowledges.

The persistence results are domain-dependent and sometimes fail outright (e.g., Math under adversarial same-domain finetuning for Qwen2.5-3B in App. A cannot recover the fingerprint even with many queries), and the paper's defense — 'the domain can be chosen a priori' — does not provide concrete, generalizable guidance for selecting domains that are robust, leaving the robustness claim only loosely substantiated.

Stealthiness claims are only qualitatively illustrated with a couple of example generations and are not stress-tested against an adversary who systematically probes multiple domains/languages and compares quality metrics (e.g., perplexity is visibly higher in the watermarked domain per Table 1, which could itself serve as a side-channel revealing which domain is being used as the fingerprint trigger); this important adaptive-adversary scenario is not addressed.

Scale of experimentation is limited to small/mid-sized models (1B and 3-7B parameters) and only three curated domains (Math, Health, French); it remains unclear how well the approach transfers to larger, more capable models or to domains that are harder to cleanly separate from general pretraining/finetuning data distributions.

The multi-watermark extension (App. C.2) shows noticeable cross-talk/confusion between different keys as more watermarks are embedded, which could be a problem for the proposed 'multi-party, multi-signature' future direction and is only lightly explored.

Minor issues: inconsistent notation in Algorithm 2 (Dreg appears twice in the 'Require' line instead of Dtarget), and some writing/typo issues (e.g., 'condicted' instead of 'conducted') suggest the manuscript would benefit from another careful proofreading pass.

strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: the paper clearly articulates practical desiderata for LLM fingerprinting (reliability, persistence, stealthiness, harmlessness, robustness) grounded in prior work and a realistic black-box threat model.

Simple yet effective core idea: restricting watermark embedding to a specific sub-domain elegantly resolves the known quality/durability trade-offs of full-coverage OSM watermarks while retaining their statistical guarantees (Type-1 error control via KGW Z-test) and monotonicity property.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across two model families (Llama3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-3B/7B) and three domains (Math, Health, French), covering detection reliability, generation quality (PPL + LLM-judge), standard benchmarks, persistence under diverse finetuning, robustness to system prompts and sampling strategies, and stealthiness.

Strong, fair head-to-head comparisons against representative backdoor-based fingerprinting baselines (Instructional Fingerprinting, Scalable Fingerprinting), showing the proposed method dominates on persistence, robustness, and stealthiness while matching reliability/harmlessness.

Extensive and thoughtful appendix experiments (watermark tokens as domain triggers, opening/closing token watermarking, multiple co-existing watermark keys, domain-leakage ablation, watermarking harmful content) that probe the boundaries and practical flexibility of the approach.
Good reproducibility practices: detailed training/eval hyperparameters, licensing information for models/datasets, and compute resource disclosure.
weaknesses: Model scale is limited to 1B–7B parameter models; it is unclear whether the domain-specific watermarking approach and its quality/robustness trade-offs generalize to larger, more capable open-source models that are more likely to be commercially deployed and worth fingerprinting.

The method requires knowledge of the deployment domain to query effectively; an adaptive adversary aware of domain-specific watermarking could restrict their served model's scope/domain coverage (e.g., only allowing English/coding queries) to sidestep a French- or Math-based fingerprint, a threat scenario not evaluated.

Persistence degrades substantially when finetuning occurs exactly within the target domain (the realistic worst case for an adversary aware of the fingerprint domain), requiring up to 1000 queries to recover detection—raising cost/practicality questions in adversarial settings beyond the toy API-cost estimate given.

Domain-leakage ablation (App. C.3) shows the method is quite sensitive to overlap between regularization and target-domain data, which is difficult to guarantee for many real-world 'domains' (e.g., topics that are not cleanly separable from general web text), somewhat undercutting practical applicability.

Math domain consistently shows the weakest watermark signal/persistence due to lower entropy, and while the authors argue domain choice mitigates this, it suggests the approach may not extend well to many technically important domains (e.g., code).

Baseline re-implementations (instructional and scalable fingerprints) were done by the authors rather than using official released fingerprinted checkpoints, which could introduce implementation bias favoring the proposed method, though the adaptations appear reasonable.

No evaluation of robustness to more aggressive/adversarial removal techniques beyond standard finetuning, such as paraphrasing attacks, quantization only briefly mentioned in the threat model but not tested, or watermark-stealing/spoofing attacks known to affect KGW-style watermarks.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated paradigm shift from brittle query-key fingerprinting to semantic-domain-conditioned statistical watermarking, addressing genuine limitations of prior work (IF, SF) in a principled way.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 3 model families/sizes, 25+ deployment scenarios (sampling, quantization, pruning, finetuning) and 5 targeted adversarial scenarios, consistently showing 100% FSR for the proposed method versus frequent failures of baselines.

Rigorous theoretical grounding: Theorem D.1 proves the Z-test statistic for concatenated multi-query detection is asymptotically standard normal, giving proper FPR control even with an added correction term beyond prior work.

Thoughtful ablations covering number of queries, semantic domain choice/entropy, watermark strength δ (utility/detectability tradeoff), and the effect of the regularization loss, which strengthen the credibility of design choices.
Reasonable effort to establish stealthiness quantitatively via an LLM-judge classifier, showing the method is far less detectable than IF and comparable to SF for inputs while remaining more robust.

Additional exploratory contributions (watermark tokens, multi-key domains, harmful-content watermarking) that expand the applicability and show extensibility of the core idea beyond the main use case.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, dataset/model licensing, resource usage, and algorithm pseudocode provided.
weaknesses: Main experiments rely heavily on a single semantic domain (French) as the primary showcase; while other domains are explored in appendices, the core narrative and most robustness claims are drawn from one setting, raising some concern about generality across languages/domains with different entropy characteristics.

Fingerprint detection cost scales with number of queries (up to 1000), and while cheap in dollar terms, this assumes the malicious deployer allows large-scale free querying without rate-limiting/cost countermeasures, which is not deeply discussed as a practical adversarial response.

Table 4 shows a non-trivial drop in LLM-as-judge quality scores within the semantic domain (e.g., LLAMA3.2-1B French score drops from 5.10 to 3.18), which, though framed as acceptable, could be a meaningful stealth/utility concern not fully reconciled with the stealth claims.

Stealth evaluation relies on a single GPT5-MINI judge with prompts chosen by the authors to minimize FPR; a more adversarial or diverse set of detectors (including ones aware of the semantic-domain concept) would strengthen the stealth claims, and the paper's own limitation section acknowledges detection is possible if the domain is known.

Model sizes tested are modest (1B–8B parameters); it is unclear how well the method scales to larger, more capable models or whether distillation-based watermark embedding remains as effective/harmless at scale.

The comparison baselines (IF, SF) were originally designed for the completion setting and adapted by the authors to the instruction-tuning setting, which could raise questions about whether the baselines were optimally tuned/implemented for a fair comparison.

strengths: Introduces a conceptually interesting new fingerprinting paradigm, replacing fixed query-key pairs with a semantic domain + statistical watermark signal, which is a reasonable and underexplored direction.

Provides a rigorous statistical justification for the detection test (Theorem D.1 with proof), giving the method principled FPR control, which is a notable strength relative to prior heuristic fingerprinting baselines.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 25 prominent deployment scenarios (quantization, pruning, sampling, system prompts, finetuning) plus 5 targeted adversarial scenarios, across three model families/sizes, consistently showing the method outperforms two recent baselines (IF, SF).
Reasonably thorough ablations (number of queries, watermark strength δ, semantic domain choice, regularization loss) that clarify trade-offs between detectability, utility, and cost.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, code provided, licenses for datasets/models listed.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a combination of existing components (Red-Green watermark, watermark distillation from Gu et al. 2024, domain-conditioned training) rather than fundamentally new machinery; novelty is primarily at the systems/paradigm level.

The stealth claim rests heavily on a single GPT5-MINI LLM-judge classifier as the only adversary model; this is a weak proxy for a determined deployer who could use other, more specialized detection strategies (the paper itself cites such specialized watermark-detection attacks but only partially addresses them).

A key limitation (acknowledged but not resolved) is that stealth and robustness depend on the adversary not knowing the chosen semantic domain; since domains like 'French' are natural, low-entropy, and guessable (especially once this methodology becomes public), an adversary could simply filter/block an entire language domain at a modest cost, which undermines the claimed robustness advantage over query-key approaches in a realistic arms-race setting.

In-domain quality degradation (notable drop in LLM-as-judge quality scores on the French domain, Table 4) suggests the watermark is not fully imperceptible within the domain, which could itself raise suspicion or usability concerns for legitimate users of that domain, partially undercutting the 'low utility impact' claim.

Detection requires up to 1000 queries to the suspicious API, which has practical costs/rate-limit implications and could itself be a detectable usage pattern (concentrated querying in a narrow domain) not evaluated as an attack surface.

Baseline comparisons (IF, SF) were adapted from their original completion-based setup to an instruction-tuned setting with un-tuned default hyperparameters, raising concerns about whether baselines were handicapped relative to the proposed method, which was tuned specifically for this setting.

Evaluation is restricted to relatively small models (1B–8B parameters); it is unclear whether findings generalize to larger, more capable models where watermark-distillation dynamics and utility trade-offs may differ.

The ethics/broader-impact discussion of potential misuse (e.g., unauthorized tracking of model usage, or false-ownership claims) is relatively shallow given the dual-use nature of covert watermarking technology.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and well-motivated paradigm for LLM fingerprinting that replaces brittle fixed query-key pairs with semantic-domain queries and statistically-grounded watermark signals, addressing real, well-documented weaknesses of prior work (IF, SF).

Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: 25 prominent deployment scenarios (sampling, quantization, pruning, finetuning) plus 5 targeted adversarial scenarios, across three model families/sizes (LLAMA3.2-1B, QWEN2.5-3B, LLAMA3.1-8B), consistently showing 100% FSR for the proposed method versus frequent failures of baselines.

Solid theoretical grounding: Theorem D.1 with a full proof shows that the proposed Z-test-based detector properly controls the false positive rate, giving the method real statistical guarantees rather than heuristic detection.

Thorough ablations covering number of queries, watermark strength (utility/detectability trade-off), choice/entropy of semantic domain, and the effect of the regularization loss, which help clarify design choices and their sensitivity.
Careful, multi-faceted stealth evaluation using an independent LLM-judge classifier, showing the fingerprint's queries/replies are much harder to detect than IF, and comparable to SF for queries.
Good scholarly positioning relative to LLM watermarking and fingerprinting literature, with clear articulation of the effectiveness/robustness/stealthiness trade-offs.
Reproducibility is well supported: detailed hyperparameters, algorithm pseudocode, released code, and licensing information for all datasets/models used.

Interesting exploratory extensions (Appendix E) on watermark tokens, multiple simultaneous keys, and watermarking harmful content, which broaden the potential impact and show flexibility of the approach beyond the core language-domain fingerprint.
weaknesses: The stealth guarantee critically depends on the adversary not knowing the chosen semantic domain; the paper acknowledges that a domain-aware adversary could simply block/filter all queries in that domain, which is a significant practical vulnerability not deeply explored (e.g., cost-benefit analysis for the adversary, or multi-domain/composed fingerprints to mitigate this).

Within the semantic domain, the fingerprint measurably degrades perceived output quality (e.g., LLM-as-a-judge scores drop noticeably, such as from 5.10 to 3.18 for LLAMA3.2-1B on French), which could itself become a stealth/utility red flag for users or deployers operating in that domain, partially undermining the stealthiness claim in that specific domain.

Detection requires on the order of 1000 queries to reliably recover the signal in adversarial settings, which, while cheap in absolute dollar terms, could raise operational concerns (e.g., rate-limiting, anomaly detection by the deployer on the querying pattern itself) that are not analyzed.

Baselines (IF, SF) were originally designed for a completion setting and had to be adapted to the instruction-tuned setting used here; while the authors are transparent about this, it introduces some risk that the baseline comparison is not entirely apples-to-apples.

The main paper focuses primarily on a single semantic domain (French) for the core experiments, with other domains (math, medicine, harmful content) relegated to the appendix as lighter-weight, less thorough validations; broader domain robustness (e.g., very narrow or very high-overlap domains with common queries) is not stress-tested as extensively.

The work relies solely on the Red-Green watermarking scheme as the statistical signal; it is unclear how sensitive the overall method's robustness/stealth trade-offs are to using alternative watermarking schemes (e.g., Gumbel/distortion-free watermarks), which could affect generality of the claims.
